title: Sentence variety with control
summary: Vary and combine sentences to express relationships clearly while preserving complete clauses, correct agreement, unambiguous reference and readable emphasis.

sections.title: Vary the thinking, not just the length
content: Sentence variety is useful when it helps the reader follow emphasis and relationships. Randomly making one sentence long and the next one short does not improve an essay. A writer first decides whether ideas are equal, dependent, contrasting, causal or descriptive, then chooses a structure that displays that relationship.

E8.1 made individual words precise. E8.2 protects that precision at sentence level: every clause must have a clear job, every joining word must express the intended link, and every pronoun and verb must still point to the correct subject after sentences are combined.

sections.title: Secure the clause before combining it
content: An independent clause can stand as a complete sentence: ‘The media club checked the audio.’ A dependent clause begins a relationship but cannot stand alone: ‘Because traffic had obscured two recordings.’ Complete the thought by adding an independent clause: ‘Because traffic had obscured two recordings, the club moved the next session.’

A fragment leaves a dependent clause or an incomplete verb group on its own. A run-on joins independent clauses without a valid boundary. A comma alone cannot normally join two independent clauses: ‘The front room faced the bus stop, the traffic drowned out two interviews’ is a comma splice.

sections.title: Let the relationship choose the structure
content: Coordinate ideas of similar weight with words such as ‘and’, ‘but’ or ‘yet’. Subordinate one idea when it supplies time, cause, condition or concession: ‘Because the front room faced a bus stop, traffic obscured parts of two recordings.’ Use a relative clause for attached identifying detail: ‘The club moved to the back room, where each interviewer tested a microphone.’

Do not stack relationship markers. ‘Because the room was noisy, so the club moved’ marks the same cause twice. Choose one grammatical route. Also avoid combining so many details that the main point disappears; a separate short sentence can give a result deliberate emphasis.

sections.title: Create emphasis through purposeful rhythm
content: A controlled paragraph may place context first, combine closely related actions, and isolate an important result: ‘The club moved its next session to a back room, where each interviewer tested a microphone before recording. The later recordings were clearer.’ The short second sentence is effective because it carries the outcome, not merely because it is short.

Vary openings only when the opening guides the reader. A time phrase can establish sequence; a dependent clause can foreground cause or contrast; an infinitive phrase can state purpose. Keep the subject first when a direct statement is clearest.

sections.title: Recheck agreement and reference
content: Combining sentences can separate a subject from its verb. Find the head subject, ignoring interrupting phrases: ‘Each of the interviewers was asked’ is singular because ‘each’ controls the verb; ‘The interviewers were asked’ is plural. Recheck every finite verb after moving or adding clauses.

Then circle each pronoun and name its exact referent. In ‘The students tested the microphones, and this improved them’, neither ‘this’ nor ‘them’ has a sufficiently clear meaning. A safer revision names the observation: ‘After the move and sound checks, the later recordings were clearer.’

sections.title: Use a four-pass control check
content: First, check boundaries: is every sentence complete, and are independent clauses joined legally? Second, check relationships: does the connector show the real logical link? Third, check control: do verbs agree with their subjects, and do pronouns have one unmistakable referent? Fourth, check emphasis: should an overloaded sentence be divided, or should two choppy sentences be combined?

Classify failures as fragment, run-on or comma splice, agreement drift, unclear reference, misleading connector or overload. Repair the named failure without changing accurate evidence merely to create a more complicated pattern.

sections.title: Control the sentence before displaying variety
content: Edit a media-club paragraph from verified notes. Make six decisions about clause completeness, causal joining, sentence boundaries, agreement, reference and purposeful rhythm. Complete the group before viewing feedback.
